source_name: Kaiten Nukariya, The Religion of the Samurai: A Study of Zen Philosophy and Discipline in China and Japan (London: Luzac & Co., 1913), Chapter I "History of Zen in China"
revision_note: Newly added with 8 verified chunks under public domain (2026-07-24, Batch 14). Source: Kaiten Nukariya's 1913 The Religion of the Samurai, Chapter I, sections 2-5 (also independently confirmed on Project Gutenberg, ebook #5173), fetched via a mirror hosting the full chapter text.

content.text: Bodhidharma came from Southern India to China in about A.D. 520. His coming was, in Nukariya's words, "the introduction, not of the dead scriptures, as was repeatedly done before him, but of a living faith, not of any theoretical doctrine, but of practical Enlightenment." He was not a teacher who courted popularity: he would not smile at any face, but stared at it with large glaring eyes, and was always clad in a faded yellow robe, indifferent to his own appearance.
content.source_name: Kaiten Nukariya, The Religion of the Samurai (1913), Chapter I

content.text: Received in audience by Emperor Wu of Liang, an enthusiastic Buddhist who had built temples and ordered monks and nuns converted, the Emperor asked whether there was merit in his conduct. "The Blue-eyed Brahmin bluntly answered: 'No merit at all.'" Pressed on the first principle of Buddhism, Bodhidharma replied: "That principle transcends all. There is nothing holy." Asked "who is that confronts us?" he answered: "I know not, your majesty."
content.source_name: Kaiten Nukariya, The Religion of the Samurai (1913), Chapter I

content.text: Finding no understanding at the Liang court, Bodhidharma left for the state of Northern Wei, where he spent nine years at the Shao Lin Monastery "mostly sitting silent in meditation with his face to the wall," earning the name "the wall-gazing Brahmin." His unpopularity among contemporary Buddhists was such that, according to his biographers, they "attempted to poison him three times, but without success."
content.source_name: Kaiten Nukariya, The Religion of the Samurai (1913), Chapter I

content.text: A Confucianist scholar, Shang Kwang, came seeking the teaching that Confucianism could not give him. Bodhidharma at first refused him entry; Shang Kwang stood in the snow-covered courtyard for seven days and nights, "with beads of the frozen drops of tears on his breast," and finally cut off his own left arm with a knife to prove his resolve. Only then did Bodhidharma admit him as a disciple.
content.source_name: Kaiten Nukariya, The Religion of the Samurai (1913), Chapter I

content.text: Shang Kwang said, "I have no peace of mind. Might I ask you, sir, to pacify my mind?" Bodhidharma replied: "Bring out your mind, here before me! I shall pacify it." After consideration, the disciple said: "It is impossible for me to seek out my mind." "Then," exclaimed Bodhidharma, "I have pacified your mind." Shang Kwang was instantly Enlightened -- a mode of instruction, Nukariya notes, that became characteristic of all Zen teaching after Bodhidharma.
content.source_name: Kaiten Nukariya, The Religion of the Samurai (1913), Chapter I

content.text: Before his death, Bodhidharma asked his disciples each to state their understanding of the Law. Tao Fu answered on the letter and the working of the Law; Bodhidharma said, "you have obtained my skin." The nun Tsung Chi answered on seeing the Buddha-kingdom once; "you have attained to my flesh." Tao Yuh spoke of the emptiness of the elements and aggregates; "you have acquired my bone." Last, Shang Kwang -- now named Hwui Ko -- simply bowed and stood silent. Bodhidharma said: "You have attained to my marrow."
content.source_name: Kaiten Nukariya, The Religion of the Samurai (1913), Chapter I

content.text: Bodhidharma handed Hwui Ko the sacred Kachaya robe he had carried from India, as a symbol of the transmission of the Law, and made him the Second Patriarch of Zen. Bodhidharma died in A.D. 528. The line he founded continued through the Second Patriarch to the Sixth, Hwui Nang, establishing the Zen lineage that would spread from China into Japan seven centuries later.
content.source_name: Kaiten Nukariya, The Religion of the Samurai (1913), Chapter I
